subject: general
question: A car is moving at a speed of 180 km/h. After the brakes are applied, it comes to a complete stop in 5 seconds. If the total mass of the car along with its passengers is 4200 kg, what is the force applied by the brakes to stop the car?
solution:
The correct answer is __**–42,000 N**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The calculation of force is based on **Newton's Second Law of Motion**, which states that **Force (F) = mass (m) × acceleration (a)**.
 
• First, we must convert the **initial velocity (u)** of the car from **km/h** to **m/s** to maintain **SI unit** consistency. Given the speed is **180 km/h**, we multiply by **5/18**. Therefore, **u = 180 × (5/18) = 50 m/s**.
 
• The car comes to a **complete stop**, which means the **final velocity (v)** is **0 m/s**. The **time (t)** taken for this change is **5 seconds**.
 
• We calculate the **acceleration (a)** using the first equation of motion: **v = u + at**. Rearranging for **a**, we get **a = (v - u) / t**. Plugging in the values: **a = (0 - 50) / 5 = -10 m/s²**. ***Hence, the acceleration is –10 m/s².***
 
• The total **mass (m)** of the system (car + passengers) is **4200 kg**. Using the force formula: **F = 4200 kg × (-10 m/s²) = -42,000 N**.
 
• The **negative sign** in the result **–42,000 N** signifies that the force is acting in the **opposite direction** to the motion of the car, which is characteristic of a **braking or retarding force**. ***Hence, the correct answer is –42,000 N.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Second Law of Motion**: This law provides a quantitative measure of force. It establishes that the **net force** acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of its **linear momentum**. For an object with a constant mass, it simplifies to the product of **mass** and **acceleration**.
 
• **Unit Conversion**: In physics problems, it is crucial to use the **International System of Units (SI)**. Velocity should be in **meters per second (m/s)**, mass in **kilograms (kg)**, and time in **seconds (s)**. The conversion factor **5/18** is derived from **1000 meters / 3600 seconds**.
 
• **Concept of Retardation**: When the velocity of an object decreases over time, the acceleration is negative. This is specifically referred to as **retardation** or **deceleration**. In this context, the brakes provide the necessary **frictional force** to cause this retardation.
 
• **The Newton (N)**: The SI unit of force is the **Newton**, named after **Sir Isaac Newton**. **1 Newton** is defined as the amount of force required to accelerate a **1 kg** mass at a rate of **1 m/s²**.
 
• **Applications**: Understanding braking force is essential in **automotive engineering** and **road safety**. It helps in determining **stopping distances** and designing efficient **braking systems** like **ABS (Anti-lock Braking System)** to handle large **inertial loads**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Momentum**: The **initial momentum** of the car was **4200 kg × 50 m/s = 210,000 kg·m/s**. The **final momentum** is **0**. The **impulse** provided by the brakes is equal to this change in momentum.
 
• **Force Direction**: Since force is a **vector quantity**, the sign is vital. A positive force would imply the car is speeding up, while the **negative force** confirms the application of brakes to reduce speed.
 
• **Mass Sensitivity**: If the **mass** of the car were lower, the same **braking force** would stop the car in **less time** or a **shorter distance**, demonstrating the role of **inertia** in motion.
